tldr: We developed DemoStream, a framework that leverages batched TAMP (Task and Motion Planning) on GPUs to simultaneously optimize massive candidate solutions, autonomously generating high-quality demonstrations ideal for imitation learning. Beyond extensive simulation benchmarks, DemoStream safely collected real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour without human teleoperation, enabling downstream policies to achieve a 67% success rate.
hero_caption: Evaluation setup with a real Franka Panda robot. Trained solely on 75 real-world demonstrations collected autonomously by DemoStream, a Diffusion Policy achieves an average success rate of 67% across three manipulation tasks: block stacking, putting a banana in the bin, and placing fruit on a plate.
overview:
Imitation learning (behavior cloning) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models hold immense promise for endowing robots with diverse manipulation skills. However, training these models demands massive amounts of demonstration data, which cannot scale if reliant entirely on human teleoperation. This has drawn significant attention to Task and Motion Planning (TAMP)—a methodology that integrates symbolic reasoning with continuous trajectory planning to solve manipulation problems autonomously.

Yet, demonstrations generated by conventional TAMP systems carry a major pitfall. Traditional search algorithms are stochastic and merely aim to find 'any single feasible solution.' As a result, the generated motions tend to be inefficient and vary widely across trials (exhibiting high multi-modality). When fed directly into standard behavior cloning pipelines, downstream policy learning often fails completely.

To overcome this, the authors introduce DemoStream, a novel TAMP system powered by modern GPU acceleration. DemoStream defines 'batched streams' that perform conditional sampling across multiple inputs simultaneously and introduces an optimization algorithm that evaluates and prunes thousands of candidate plans over a unified computational graph. This enables the rapid generation of clean, consistent, and easy-to-imitate demonstrations for downstream robot policies.

Extensive simulation ablation studies reveal that while unoptimized traditional TAMP demonstrations yield a 0% policy success rate, DemoStream's demonstrations—optimized to minimize task-space end-effector motion—achieve remarkably high success rates. Furthermore, in real-world environments, DemoStream safely collected demonstrations autonomously at an average rate of 66 demos per hour without human intervention during execution, successfully training high-performing visuomotor policies using real data alone.
contributions: Proposed 'batched streams' and a computational graph optimization algorithm that fully leverage GPU acceleration to search and optimize thousands of candidate plans in parallel.
Established an end-to-end pipeline that autonomously generates high-quality demonstrations for training visuomotor policies without requiring any human teleoperation.

Systematically analyzed the impact of action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes on downstream imitation learning success rates, identifying the minimization of task-space end-effector motion as a crucial factor.

Demonstrated applicability across multi-arm coordination, long-horizon tasks, and LLM-guided open-world settings, while achieving autonomous real-world demonstration collection at an average rate of 66 demos per hour.

sections.heading: Why Do Policies Fail to Learn from Traditional TAMP Demonstrations?
sections.summary: Training robot foundation models requires massive demonstration datasets, but manual teleoperation hits scalability limits. While TAMP can autonomously generate motion plans, existing planners produce highly inconsistent solutions that lead to imitation learning failure. This work introduces DemoStream, using GPU-batched optimization to automatically generate learnable, high-quality demonstrations.
sections.details:
Foundation models such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures are transforming robot learning, but unlocking their potential requires vast amounts of robot interaction data. While manual teleoperation is an intuitive collection method, it incurs substantial human labor costs for every new task and does not scale. Semi-automated techniques that adapt a handful of human demonstrations to new scenes have emerged, but they still demand manual per-task annotation and struggle with safety guarantees.

This makes Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) an appealing alternative, as the same domain models can autonomously solve previously unseen tasks. In theory, TAMP could continuously generate infinite demonstrations. In practice, however, prior attempts to train policies on TAMP demos have struggled. Traditional TAMP algorithms rely on stochastic search; their goal is purely satisficing, which produces non-optimal trajectories with huge variance (multi-modal solution distributions) across runs.

Here lies the core insight: successful imitation learning (behavior cloning) does not merely require trajectories that solve the task; it requires trajectories that are consistent with respect to states and free of unnecessary motions. Rather than using GPU parallelism solely to solve TAMP faster, the authors leverage GPU compute to optimize demonstration quality across thousands of candidate solutions. This unlocks successful visuomotor policy learning across multi-arm coordination, long-horizon tasks, open-world settings, and even fully autonomous real-world data collection.

sections.heading: Prior Limitations: Human-Dependent Demos vs. 'Satisficing-Only' TAMP
sections.summary: Prior demo-generation methods adapt human seed demonstrations, but they struggle with novel objects and altered task structures. Meanwhile, existing TAMP-based demo collection frameworks neglect plan optimization, making downstream learning difficult. DemoStream eliminates human seed demonstrations entirely, directly optimizing demonstrations for downstream learnability.
sections.details:
### Demonstration Generation for Imitation Learning
To reduce human effort in training visuomotor policies via Behavior Cloning (BC), demonstration adaptation frameworks like MimicGen transform a small set of teleoperated demos to match new initial configurations, filtering for successful rollouts. However, when initial scenes vary substantially, obstacle arrangements and safe collision-free paths shift drastically, causing transformation failure. Other works incorporate motion planning, but they remain fundamentally task-dependent: every new procedure or object requires a human to provide initial demonstrations. DemoStream, by contrast, requires zero human seed demonstrations and autonomously plans for novel objects and task layouts from scratch.

### Task and Motion Planning (TAMP)
TAMP integrates discrete decisions (e.g., which object to grasp) with continuous trajectory generation (e.g., moving arms while avoiding collisions). Recent systems such as cuTAMP and ScheduleStream harness GPUs to accelerate continuous parameter search, but GPU acceleration has predominantly focused on fast collision checking for multi-arm systems.

While earlier research investigated using TAMP for automated demonstration generation, those approaches relied on conventional CPU-based algorithms that merely search for 'any single feasible solution.' The crucial concept of optimizing for demonstration 'learnability' was missing. Furthermore, no prior work demonstrated a safe, scalable, and fully autonomous TAMP data collection pipeline on physical robots.

sections.heading: Unlocking GPUs with 'Batched Streams' and Computational Graph Optimization
sections.summary: Traditional TAMP samplers operate on single inputs, failing to exploit GPU parallelism. DemoStream defines 'batched streams' to process large batches of inputs simultaneously and couples them with a lazy-evaluation computational graph optimization algorithm. This allows the system to rapidly identify the minimal-cost plan out of thousands of candidates.
sections.details:
### III-A TAMP Foundations
DemoStream builds upon ScheduleStream, a domain-independent specification language supporting continuous sampling. Extending classical PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language), continuous quantities such as robot joint configurations $q \in \mathbf{R}^d$ and object grasp poses $g \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ are sampled via Python-based samplers called streams. For instance, in a task where two blocks are placed onto a plate, actions such as 'move', 'pick', and 'place' are declared with preconditions (cond), effects (eff), and additive transition costs (cost).

### III-B Batched Streams
Traditional streams take a single input tuple and sample an output tuple. Consequently, they cannot interface with modern batched inverse kinematics (IK) solvers capable of evaluating, say, 128 grasp-placement pairs simultaneously. To resolve this, the authors introduce the 'BatchStream.' A BatchStream consumes a list of input tuples and utilizes GPU parallelism to generate a batch of candidate outputs up to a maximum batch size (e.g., $N=128$). In this work, placement pose generation, IK solving, collision checking, and motion trajectory generation are all batched.

### III-C Batched Planning Algorithm
To solve batched streams efficiently, the authors developed the 'batch-stream' algorithm. It first conducts a lightweight finite search using placeholder variables to discover a symbolic skeleton plan $\pi$. From this, it constructs a computational graph (stream plan $\psi$) tracking parameter dependencies across actions.

Next, the core subroutine, 'batch-optimization,' is invoked. It executes each batched stream in topological order, progressively updating parameter bindings. For example, if there are 1,000 grasp candidates and 1,000 placement candidates, their Cartesian product is massive. DemoStream sorts these intermediate bindings by accumulated partial cost (such as workspace displacement) and passes only the top-128 most promising candidates to the batched IK stream on the GPU. This greedy filtering prevents memory explosion while enabling the planner to isolate the lowest-cost, optimal motion plan $b_*$ from thousands of possibilities in fractions of a second.

captions.F2: Overview of the batched IK stream (ik_qs). It takes up to 128 inverse kinematics subproblems—formed by paired grasp and placement poses—as a single input batch, and simultaneously computes and returns a list of valid joint configurations $q$.
captions.F3: Batched computational graph (stream plan $\psi$) for picking and placing a block onto a plate. As execution proceeds from grasp/placement sampling through IK, collision checking, and trajectory generation, batched streams are invoked and sorted/filtered by cost, ultimately converging to the optimal plan.

sections.heading: The Secret to Learnable Demos: Minimizing Task-Space End-Effector Motion
sections.summary: We built a pipeline that trains behavior cloning policies on autonomously generated TAMP demonstrations. Minimizing task-space end-effector displacement proved vital as a planning cost function to reduce demonstration variance. Furthermore, an LLM coding agent enables the pipeline to handle open-world, natural language goal instructions.
sections.details:
### IV-A Demonstration Generation Pipeline
Demonstrations record robot proprioception (joint positions, end-effector poses) along with RGB images from a wrist-mounted camera and an external camera. Three action spaces were evaluated: absolute joint positions (Joint-Abs), relative joint positions (Joint-Rel), and relative task-space end-effector poses tracked by an IK controller (IK-Rel). For each task, 1,000 successful demonstration episodes were collected to train supervised models including BC-RNN and Diffusion Policy. A parallelized simulator (IsaacLab) was employed to prevent environment stepping bottlenecks.

### IV-B Stream Implementations
For robot and obstacle collision checking, meshes are approximated using spheres and processed at high throughput on the GPU via cuRoboV2. Grasp samplers generate 10,000 candidate grasps along antipodal surfaces using vectorized operations, rapidly filtering them via fingertip sphere collision checks.

### IV-C Cost Function Design and Hypothesis
A pivotal design choice in TAMP is the cost function used to select trajectories. Three configurations were compared:
- Zero cost (Zero): Any feasible plan is accepted, mirroring standard satisficing TAMP.
- Joint-space distance (Joint): Minimizes total robot joint displacement.
- Task-space distance (Task): Minimizes the total translation and rotation of the end-effector link.
The hypothesis behind the task-space cost is that minimizing end-effector movement minimizes camera jitter and visual shifts from the wrist-mounted camera. This drastically narrows the distribution of visual observations that downstream policies must learn to handle.

### IV-D Motion Planner Selection
For low-level trajectory generation, the framework supports cuRoboV2's optimization solver alongside a GPU-batched PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) planner with trajectory shortcutting. A task-space variant, T-PRM, was introduced to plan directly in end-effector space.

### IV-E Goal Generation via LLM Agents
To handle natural language instructions (e.g., 'place the Rubik's cube to the left of the bowl'), an LLM coding agent generates vectorized goal evaluation functions. Because the generated code is compatible with GPU-batched planning, the system effortlessly adapts to open-world goal specifications.

sections.heading: Plan Optimization Catapults Policy Success Rates from 0% to 90%
sections.summary: Extensive experiments were conducted in simulation and on real hardware. Unoptimized traditional TAMP demonstrations resulted in a 0% policy success rate, whereas task-space optimization elevated success to 90%. On a real Franka Panda robot, DemoStream collected 66 demonstrations per hour autonomously, achieving an average policy success rate of 67%.
sections.details:
### V-A Ablations on Action Spaces and Cost Functions
In the Stack-Three task (stacking three blocks), BC-RNN policies were trained across different demo configurations. The contrast was striking: demonstrations collected using Zero cost (satisficing TAMP) produced a 0% policy success rate in both Joint-Abs and Joint-Rel action spaces. In contrast, when DemoStream minimized task-space cost (Task + T-PRM), policies across all action spaces achieved strong performance. With Diffusion Policy, success reached 90% for Joint-Rel and 86% for Joint-Abs and IK-Rel. Preventing unnecessary wrist camera movement proved decisive for visual imitation learning.

### V-B Comparison with Existing Demo Generation (MimicGen)
Comparing DemoStream against MimicGen (which adapts human seed demos), MimicGen struggled with wide initial scene variations, securing only a 35% demo collection success rate and requiring 9 seconds per successful demonstration. DemoStream achieved a 92% collection success rate at 6 seconds per demonstration. Furthermore, policies trained on DemoStream data consistently outperformed those trained on MimicGen, highlighting DemoStream's edge alongside its total elimination of human annotation.

### V-C Scaling Batch Sizes
Scaling the batched IK stream size from 1 to 256 not only improved demo collection success rates, but also significantly shortened average demonstration lengths and reduced standard deviations. Policies trained on demos from batch size 1 (resembling CPU-based TAMP) achieved only ~34% success, whereas batch size 256 pushed success to 86%. Expanding the search candidate pool directly lowers trajectory variance, unlocking superior downstream policy learning.

### V-D Complex TAMP Tasks
DemoStream was evaluated on challenging manipulation problems: 4-block stacking (Stack-Four), stacking inside an occluded box (Bin-Stack), bi-manual collaboration (Multi-Arm), and packing objects around obstacles (Pack-Two). Across all setups, DemoStream maintained high demo collection rates (80–96%) and yielded high-performing downstream policies.

### V-E Complex Geometries and Open-World Goals
In the RoboLab environment featuring everyday objects (bananas, mustard bottles, Rubik's cubes) and natural language goals, DemoStream performed robustly. Although complex geometries required repeated sampling iterations to find stable grasps, the downstream policies trained on these rollouts maintained strong success rates.

### V-F Real-Robot Autonomous Data Collection and Evaluation
Using a real Franka Panda arm and a DROID-style setup, DemoStream was deployed on three physical tasks: block stacking, putting a banana in a bin, and placing fruit on a plate. Object geometries were segmented from point clouds using SAM3, and demonstrations were collected autonomously from command-line task prompts. Human involvement was restricted purely to resetting initial object states and labeling success/failure; no safety halts occurred, yielding an autonomous collection speed of 66 demos per hour. A Diffusion Policy trained solely on 75 collected demos achieved an average success rate of 67% on the real robot.

captions.F5: Challenging stacking tasks used for evaluation: long-horizon 4-block stacking (Stack-Four, left), 3-block stacking inside an obstructing bin (Stack-Bin, center), and bi-manual collaborative 3-block stacking (Multi-Arm, right). DemoStream successfully generated high-quality demonstrations for all three.
captions.F1: Evaluation on a physical Franka Panda arm. A Diffusion Policy trained exclusively on 75 real-world demonstrations collected by DemoStream achieves an average success rate of 67% across three manipulation tasks: block stacking, putting a banana in a bin, and placing fruit on a plate.

takeaways: For autonomous demonstration generation in imitation learning, mere feasibility is insufficient; optimizing candidate plans to eliminate trajectory multi-modality is essential for downstream policy convergence.
When training visuomotor policies—especially on arms equipped with eye-in-hand wrist cameras—minimizing task-space end-effector motion is far more effective than joint-space cost functions.
Directing GPU compute toward solution optimization shrinks high-quality TAMP search times from minutes to seconds, establishing a viable, human-free data collection pipeline for real-world robotics.
limitations: In real-world experiments, human operators were still required to reset object layouts and label episode success/failure (though authors note these steps could be automated for certain tasks).
For complex everyday object geometries, iterative rejection sampling for stable grasps can increase planning latency.
Cost functions that aggressively dampen end-effector movement to stabilize wrist camera views may require further validation in contact-rich manipulation tasks, such as compliant insertions.
